highlights.title: Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem
highlights.summary: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis. A mathematician at Anthropic has convincingly said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved…
body: Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks.
On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution.

The proof evidently marks another breakthrough in the use of AI for complicated math problems – even as mathematicians express uneasiness around extremely lucrative private companies dishing out millions of dollars for the technology to solve problems.

“Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line,” Alpöge wrote, while anthropomorphizing the AI software. “No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”

body: After hard-fought 1-0 wins against Manchester City last Saturday and Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday night, Chelsea drew a blank. Against Gareth Taylor’s side, Chelsea’s lack of cutting edge was clear a week after beating City to go top. The calf injury picked up by Melvine Malard against City, the absence of Lauren James, who has a thigh injury, and the form of Aggie Beever-Jones, who scored her first WSL goal in more than a year in the 6-0 defeat of Charlton, have left Chelsea’s attack short.

Despite almost 70% possession and 47 touches in the box to Liverpool’s 12, Sonia Bompastor’s side amassed only 19 shots to Liverpool’s 13 and seven on target to their opponents’ four. Although the Blues remain unbeaten in the WSL, their third draw in five games in all competitions means City can leapfrog them at the top if they beat Tottenham on Sunday.
Liverpool had chances, particularly in the first half, but were hanging on after the break and Keating helped them to a fourth clean sheet, a tally bettered only by Bompastor’s side.

highlights.title: All Cheat Codes in GTA 6
highlights.summary: The best part about any Grand Theft Auto game is the cheats, and Grand Theft Auto 6 delivers on that front. Rockstar's latest includes a whole mess of password-protected secrets that will really let you have some fun in Vice City. You'll have to work for them, though.
body: Here's everything you need to know about cheats in GTA 6, from how to unlock them, to the list itself.
Update (Nov. 21): We've updated this guide with inputs for three cheat codes.

If you're looking for a way to enter cheat codes the moment you start GTA 6, you're going to be disappointed. You won't be able to use them until you have fully cleared the story. Once you finish the game and return to your save file, you'll find a new Cheat tab. Open your Map, tab over to Progression, and scroll to the end to find the Cheats menu.

You won't get the actual cheat codes immediately. Each one is locked behind a requirement. That can be as simple as finding a specific car to earn the ability to summon it, or as demanding as having Jason and Lucia hold hands for four hours. Once you clear a condition, a pop-up message will tell you that you've unlocked a new Cheat code, and the unlock requirement in the Cheats menu will be replaced with the code.

highlights.title: The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’
highlights.summary: One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called "killer robots." Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to "start discussing options" after a largely fruitless week of…
body: Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.

The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”

Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

body: After six deflating losses in a row to South Africa, New Zealand and France, Andy Farrell was asked this week what made him think Ireland could get back to the levels they had reached when considered squarely among that group.
Because they had got there before came the typically uncomplicated response from the side's head coach.

The longer the 2023 World Cup receded into memory, however, fewer and fewer believed that his side still had within them the type of performance they produced to beat the Springboks 20-17 on Saturday.

Undoubtedly Ireland's biggest win of recent years, having not beaten one of the three sides who started this weekend above them in the rankings since the summer of 2024, this was one of their most needed too.

highlights.title: The Australian fashion artisans who still make clothes by hand
highlights.summary: The meticulous process of hand-stitching clothing and footwear is rare in Australia, but the ateliers who do so are attracting a new generation of clients and colleagues. Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email.
body: In a world where garment makers are forced to wear AI-training headgear and T-shirts can be ordered from Kmart on Uber Eats, it may seem as if the days of procuring something made by hand from an artisan are numbered.

While jobs in Australian textile, clothing and footwear manufacturing have been in freefall since their 1989 peak – from 115,000 to approximately 30,000 in 2026 – the work of a dressmaker or shoemaker who stitches every piece by hand is even harder to find.
But in certain studios and fitting rooms around the country, tape measures are wielded, fabric is pinched and pinned and the warmth of service extends well beyond holding out an Eftpos machine.

For hand-makers, the work is about more than just another product or a paycheck. The beauty of their vocation is in many small acts: mastering technique, appreciating texture, building a community of clients, and drawing on the mysterious well of creative intuition that allows humans to make wonderful things.

highlights.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
highlights.summary: An actor has licensed his face to a microdrama startup — in a trend that's already popular in China. Experts question the long-term consequences if this becomes a trend in Hollywood, too.
body: For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.

The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.

Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”

Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.
points: An actor has licensed his face to a microdrama startup — in a trend that's already popular in China.
Experts question the long-term consequences if this becomes a trend in Hollywood, too.

highlights.title: The moment I knew: She flew me to the scene of my favourite romantic movie
highlights.summary: Kaz Therese had always loved An Affair to Remember. A few months into their relationship, Brianna surprised her with a magical gift. Find more stories from the moment I knew series.
body: Brianna and I met in 2013 on an arts project I was developing in Mount Druitt, the region I grew up in, in western Sydney.
It was a site-specific work for young people, and Brianna became part of the strategic leadership team, which ultimately meant she was painting gutters pink with the local kids until 9pm each night.

Our first meeting was electric – we had so much in common, I felt like I’d been donged on the head. Through the work, I was trying to push back against the stigma of Mount Druitt and create something fun and magical, and she understood the importance of what I was trying to do. After the project, I got a position running a theatre company in Fairfield, also in western Sydney, and I invited her on to the board.

We were both in relationships at the time, I was coming out of a deeply unhappy one. For those first two years working together, I had a secret crush on her. A few months later we were both single and I invited her over to do some work writing a grant together for a project I hoped to do in Berlin. That week happened to be my birthday, and a friend had given me a bottle of Moët, which I planned to save for a special occasion.

highlights.title: Cops Are Pushing Extremely Corny ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Slop
highlights.summary: The blockbuster game makes no secret of its contempt for law enforcement. Real police departments using it to recruit new members and scold the public apparently didn’t get the memo.
body: Listening to the in-game radio stations while you cruise around in Grand Theft Auto VI, you might hear a recruitment ad for the Vice City Police Department, which makes no secret of the kind of maladjusted psychos it's looking for.

“Have you always dreamed of abusing your power without consequence?” one spot begins. “Well, now you can, when you join the Vice City Police Department, VCPD. You’ll have fun learning the ins and outs of applying excessive force.” The commercial goes on to suggest that cadets will be trained in racial profiling and planting evidence.

Given that blistering analysis of American law enforcement, you might imagine that actual cops aren’t big fans of the latest GTA title, which was released after a 13-year wait on Thursday. Yet as millions of gamers have started to explore every stash house and back alley in the sun-drenched wilderness of a fictionalized South Florida, even police departments have attempted to exploit this monocultural mania to elevate their public messaging or recruit new officers.

highlights.title: It’s Official, GTA 6’s Graphics Have Broken My Brain
highlights.summary: The first time I played Grand Theft Auto 5, I was ready to wreak havoc the second I picked up the controller. When my buddy handed me the controller to try it out at his apartment, I asked him how to unlock all weapons and got up to the old tricks of my PS2 glory days.
body: The first time I played Grand Theft Auto 6 was a very different experience. Immediately taken aback by its comparatively ultrarealistic visuals, all of my usual GTA instincts went haywire. For the first time ever in one of these games, I found myself instinctively following traffic laws. I didn’t consider running a red light. I was patiently waiting in traffic jams. I wouldn’t even dare to bump another car and risk scratching up my paint. Killing a pedestrian? Absolutely not!

I’m not the only one who has experienced this phenomenon, as I’ve since discovered. PC Gamer’s Lincoln Carpenter recalled having the exact same experience in GTA 6. I’ve heard some of my colleagues say the same thing upon starting the game themselves. [ Ed. note: Confirmed.] It’s undeniable that GTA 6 ’s shift towards realistic visuals comes with some psychological side effects. In my review, I argued that the shift in mentality ends up being to GTA 6 ’s benefit as it plays into the rule-breaking joys of the series. But it does beg a tired question that feels older than GTA itself at this point: How real is too real?

body: After a tribute video showcased iconic Goldblum performances across his career, including roles in “Invasion of the Body Snatchers,” “The Fly,” “Jurassic Park” and “Independence Day,” the curtain rose to reveal the actor — an accomplished pianist and jazz musician — seated behind a grand piano, from which he performed a medley of songs before a rapt crowd.

Accepting the award after a lengthy standing ovation, Goldblum thanked the many screenwriters, directors and actors who showed faith in him through the years and insisted that moviemaking remains as vital an art form as ever.

“I believe that the stories that we tell matter,” the actor said. “At their best, films let us sit in the dark beside strangers and see the world through somebody else’s eyes. They remind us that we lucky creatures have an unfathomable measure of commonality, and they put to shame all those petty things which seem to divide us.

“Movies also help us imagine something better — a world that works for everyone,” he continued. “That’s a planet toward which I want to keep working for as long as I have breath in my body, and with every story that I might still have the privilege to tell.”

highlights.summary: Exotic lawns require a tradeoff between ease and beauty. While Australian native grasses take longer to establish, they can be worth the wait. Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email. Do you yearn for that suburban dream, the perfect lawn?
body: Do you yearn to join one of those neighbourhood groups whose members compete to show off the result – the kind of people who use laser levels and precision bombing with biological weapons to achieve grassy perfection?
“There’s no grass that ticks all the boxes,” says Melbourne landscaper Simon McCurdy. “Each has its positive attributes and drawbacks.”

In his 38 years of experience, McCurdy has seen roll-out turf largely displace seed-sowing for lawn establishment. “Virtually all our clients want instant results,” he says. “And when you factor in the time involved in sowing from seed it’s certainly cheaper for most people to install turf.”

For larger areas McCurdy says many people choose hydroseeding, an intermediate method between seeding and turf, in which emulsions of seed, water, mulch and fertiliser are sprayed on to prepared soil. But which grass variety to choose?

highlights.title: Q&A: Enabling more human-like interactions and understanding in multimodal foundation models
highlights.summary: Senior Research Scientist Jim Glass discusses how his MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab collaboration connects perception and language, and addresses the shortcoming of current models.
body: Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples.

Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview.

highlights.title: International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
highlights.summary: Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’ Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome…
body: Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.

Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.

Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a new law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.

highlights.title: New approach enables physically consistent AI models of chaotic systems
highlights.summary: Enforcing physics-based constraints prevents AI models from generating unreliable predictions for complex nonlinear systems in weather, climate, and turbulent flows.
body: Modeling of complex, chaotic processes such as weather and climate patterns and turbulent flows in aviation or in ocean currents has advanced enormously in recent years. However, such models are still prone to drift into physically impossible predictions over time.

Now, researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models that can ensure that such models never exceed realistic bounds, based on what is actually possible in the real world. This new approach, using information that is now being made freely available by the team, could significantly improve the usefulness and reliability of such models, which besides climate and weather are also used in a wide range of industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology.
The new findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis.

body: Doué went down after twisting awkwardly late in the first half as he tried to control the ball, shortly after scoring to put PSG 2-1 ahead. He looked to be in agony as he clutched his right knee, and the match was stopped for five minutes to allow Doué to receive treatment before being carried off to a backdrop of applause from the crowd at the Allianz Riviera stadium.

PSG will now be dreading discovering the extent of the injury, having lost Khvicha Kvaratskhelia to a ruptured anterior cruciate ligament in his right knee playing against Barcelona last month. The Georgian winger is unlikely to return this season, and Doué looks set for a significant spell on the sidelines too.
“We will need to wait until tomorrow for the test results, but it is obviously a serious injury,” PSG’s coach, Luis Enrique, told the broadcaster Ligue 1+.
Mohamed Amoura had given Nice the lead only for Senny Mayulu to equalise with a penalty awarded after a video assistant referee check for a handball.

"So then, I get a chip, and it's like, 'What does this let me do?' Immediately, controlling a computer is like, 'boom.' Portal to the world. You just immediately get your portal to the world back."

Rockstar spent 13 years painstakingly crafting the world of GTA 6 to ensure every blade of grass and every line of dialogue was given an unprecedented amount of detail. Although it's maybe truer to life than some may have hoped, there's no denying that the amount of freedom the studio gives players to do everything from robbing banks to diving for sunken treasure has attracted tens of millions of players.

Despite guiding Jason and Lucia through GTA 6 by different means, the Neuralink participant shown today is one of those millions. In a follow-up post, the tech company, which was co-founded by controversial figure and billionaire Elon Musk, reiterated that the participant and others like him are part of an extremely limited clinical trial.

highlights.summary: Amid allegations of multiple affairs, including with a direct report and an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, sources tell WIRED the Nvidia board’s main issue was the former CEO’s “lack of candor.”
body: Jensen Huang was ousted from Nvidia amid allegations of extramarital affairs, including a relationship with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset. Yet it was “multiple issues” related to Huang’s “lack of candor” and “lying” that ultimately moved the board of directors, according to two people familiar with private discussions among the chair and other members.

While Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang on November 8, the board couldn’t determine in the moment whether she was an intelligence operative for China, these sources say. That same day, the board announced an independent investigation “in light of recent reporting” that their CEO had “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has rejected allegations that Alice Huang was a spy.

But in the following days, once allegations of other affairs surfaced, including one reportedly with a direct report, “what could be determined was [Huang’s] lying, and that spanned a year, from October 2025 through recent events,” a source close to the board told WIRED, who requested anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak on its behalf.
